result.summary: Iole tells Alcmena how her sister Dryope plucked flowers from a lotus that was really the nymph Lotis, and was turned into a tree herself. Iolaüs then appears, made young again by Hebe, and Themis prophesies coming wars and the sudden growing up of Calirrhoë's sons. The other gods complain that they cannot grant such gifts.

scenes.title: Iole begins her sister's tale
scenes.summary: Alcmena sighs for her old servant, and Iole offers to tell of her own sister Dryope. Dryope was wronged by Apollo and then married Andræmon.

scenes.title: Dryope plucks the lotus
scenes.summary: At a lake Dryope picks lotus flowers for her son and sees blood drip from them. She is rooted and covered with bark, while her family comes and clings to her.
scenes.stakes: Dryope is losing her human body and her child's nursing.

scenes.title: Dryope's last words
scenes.summary: Dryope swears she is innocent, asks that her son be cared for and taught to revere shrubs, and says farewell as the bark closes over her.
scenes.stakes: Dryope is dying as the bark covers her, and she fears for her child.

scenes.title: Iolaüs returns young; Themis prophesies
scenes.summary: Iolaüs appears rejuvenated by Hebe. Themis stops Hebe from swearing never to do it again and foretells Theban wars and Calirrhoë's sons.
scenes.stakes: The future of Thebes and Orestes-like vengeance are foretold, with grief ahead for Alcmæon.

scenes.title: The gods complain
scenes.summary: The gods murmur that they cannot grant the same gift. Aurora, Ceres, Mulciber and Venus each ask for a loved one.

notable_quotes.reason: Dryope's simple protest of innocence before she is lost.

analysis.text: Innocent people are punished for the acts of gods and the transformations of others, as Dryope pays for Lotis's flight.
The passage links grief with rejuvenation and prophecy, moving the book toward the question of age and fate.

legacy.text: Dryope's tale belongs to the tradition of women turned into trees, which later poets such as Dante echoed with the wood of suicides.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's version differs from other accounts, in which Dryope was taken by nymphs and a poplar sprang up in her place.

language_notes.text: Iole means Alcmena grieves even for a servant whose body was transformed, though she was no blood relation; 'alien to thy blood' means unrelated.
Œchalian refers to Œchalia, a city in Greece associated with king Eurytus, Dryope's father.
'The God that owns Delphi and Delos' is Apollo, whose chief sanctuaries were at Delphi and on the island of Delos.
'Tyrian tints' means purple-red, the famous dye from Tyre; the lotus flower is compared to it.
'Swains' are country people or shepherds, here the local source of the story.
'Groin' here means the lower body at the hips; the bark climbs upward from the legs.
"If any credit is to be given to the wretched" means: if the unfortunate deserve to be believed at all, accept my oath.
Dryope became a tree after unknowingly plucking blossoms from a lotus that was the transformed nymph Lotis, hence her warning about ponds, flowers and shrubs.
Themis foretells the war of the Seven against Thebes: Capaneus struck down by Jupiter's thunderbolt, Eteocles and Polynices killing each other, Amphiaraüs swallowed alive by the earth.
The son is Alcmaeon, who killed his mother Eriphyle to avenge his father Amphiaraüs. The fatal gold is the necklace of Harmonia; Phegeus' sons kill him.
Hebe is Jupiter's daughter and Hercules' wife, so she is his daughter and also, through Hercules, his daughter-in-law; Juno is her mother, hence "step-daughter" as the translator renders it.
Each god asks for a mortal favourite: Aurora's husband Tithonus, Ceres' lover Iäsion, Venus' lover Anchises, and Mulciber's (Vulcan's) foster-son Ericthonius.

context_notes.text: Iole speaks as Alcmena's daughter-in-law, being married to Alcmena's son Hyllus.
Nymphs, here the Naiads, were female spirits of water and trees; people brought them garlands and offerings at springs and lakes.
Priapus was a rustic god of fertility, usually shown as lustful and ridiculous. Lotis fled him and became a lotus tree.
Iolaüs was the nephew and companion of Hercules, who was Alcmena's son. He had grown old, so his sudden youth astonishes the women.
Themis is the goddess of divine order and justice, and she is known for prophecy.
Aurora is the dawn goddess. Her husband Tithonus was granted immortality but not eternal youth, so he withered with age.

literary_notes.text: The narrator's remark about Dryope's unsuspecting approach and her coming offering hints at a cruel, ironic fate.
Blood dripping from flowers and trembling boughs makes the plant disturbingly alive, revealing the hidden human victim.
The switch to the present tense makes the transformation immediate and vivid, as though Iole is reliving it.
Iole addresses her absent sister directly, intensifying the grief and her own helplessness.
The image of only a face still human, with the rest tree, ends the scene on stark, poignant loss.
Her fate is punishment, yet she has committed no crime, a stark contrast that underscores the injustice of the metamorphosis.
The bark "creeping" and enveloping her gives the transformation a slow, stealthy life of its own.
The repeated "at once" joins speech and existence, so that her voice and life end together.
The gods are shown murmuring and quarrelling like humans, a gently humorous touch that makes divine favouritism petty.
